comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C1, C21-C23. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find the behavioral paradigm (habituation and O-bend response) well-supported and established. Both describe the data as solid/valuable with no substantive concerns.

Strong agreement on claims C2-C5, C31-C33. Both evaluations support the identification of functional clusters with divergent responses through calcium imaging. OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive methodology (30,890±3,235 ROIs, 12 clusters), while peer reviewers describe the findings as 'intriguing' and 'valuable,' though one notes concerns about visual cue responses lowering clarity.

Partial overlap on claims C24-C30 (imaging methodology and anatomical findings). Both evaluations support the imaging approach. OpenEval focuses on technical details and spatial segregation, while peer reviewers emphasize the methodological platform's uniqueness but note concerns about mixed responses to irrelevant visual cues.

Perfect agreement on claims C6, C36-C37, C39-C41. Both evaluations support the screening approach as valuable. OpenEval emphasizes validation through re-identification of known modulators and the 9% hit rate, while peer reviewers note the paradigm is valuable though 'not novel.'

Significant disagreement on claims C9, C42-C47, C65-C67 regarding PTX and GABAergic inhibition. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with acknowledgment of potential off-target effects, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN with substantial concerns about interpretation. Peer reviewers provide multiple alternative explanations (neural noise, sensory processing disruption) and emphasize that 'a clear interpretation...has not been established.'

Perfect agreement on claims C7, C48-C50. Both evaluations support melatonin findings positively. OpenEval emphasizes specificity of effect on response probability versus displacement, while peer reviewers describe melatonin as 'potentially new contributions' and part of 'interesting new molecular pathways.'

Agreement on claims C8, C51 regarding oestrogen receptor agonists. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to less clear specificity and effects on other behaviors, while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, viewing the findings as 'potentially new contributions' alongside melatonin. Peer reviewers appear more positive despite OpenEval's specificity concerns.

Perfect agreement on claims C10, C53-C57. Both evaluations support the finding that pharmacological treatments shift cluster proportions without changing average response profiles. Both acknowledge this as a negative result showing no simple relationship between interventions and outcomes. OpenEval notes technical limitations of head-restrained protocol, while peer reviewers describe the link as 'not especially convincing.'

Perfect agreement on claims C11, C79, C89. Both evaluations support the overarching conclusion about complexity of habituation circuits and mechanisms. OpenEval synthesizes evidence across behavioral, pharmacological, and imaging experiments, while peer reviewers explicitly accept that 'circuits and mechanisms...are likely more complex than anticipated.'

Agreement on claim C60 as speculative. Both rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval emphasizes insufficient evidence for causality regarding cluster 4 neurons being 'most critical,' while peer reviewers note this falls under general critique that 'a clear interpretation...has not been established' and requires more testing of alternative models.

Partial overlap on claims C68-C69 (Drosophila comparison). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED as appropriate contextualization, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, challenging mechanistic interpretation and noting alternative models have not been tested. Disagreement centers on whether comparative argument is sufficiently supported.

Strong agreement on claims C70-C75 (public health context). Both evaluations support these literature-based contextual claims. OpenEval notes appropriate citations, while peer reviewers view pathway identification positively as 'useful to guide follow-up experiments.' No substantive concerns from either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on claims C80-C82. Both evaluations support the discussion of prior work and potential explanations for differences. OpenEval describes speculation as reasonable and appropriately tentative, while peer reviewers implicitly accept novelty by noting potentiation and no-adaptation clusters 'have not been previously observed.'

Perfect agreement on claims C84, C86-C88. Both evaluations support these anatomical and literature-based contextual claims without challenge. OpenEval notes appropriate citations to prior studies, while peer reviewers accept anatomical localization as part of 'valuable' imaging data.

Perfect agreement on claims C12-C20. Both evaluations support this background framing of the field. OpenEval notes well-established facts with appropriate citations, while peer reviewers explicitly accept that 'habituation being a form of learning widespread in the animal kingdom, the investigation of neural mechanisms...is a worthwhile endeavor.'

Perfect agreement on claims C90-C96. Both evaluations support the methodological details and exclusion criteria. OpenEval notes transparent reporting of high exclusion rate (39%), while peer reviewers describe imaging approach as having 'great potential' and note experiments 'cannot be achieved currently in other vertebrate systems.' No criticism of exclusion rate from either.

OpenEval result R16 addresses claim C78 (prior model from Randlett et al., 2019) as appropriate citation of prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific contextual claim.

Minor overlap on claims C66-C67 regarding PTX effects and GABAergic mechanisms. OpenEval R4 rates PTX findings as SUPPORTED with caveats about off-target effects, while peer R11 rates mechanistic interpretation as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing that alternative models where 'inhibition is not required for habituation, have not been fully tested.' Disagreement on strength of mechanistic conclusions.
